statement: In 30 adults seeking outpatient treatment for heavy cocaine use in New Haven, mostly men in their twenties and thirties who used in binges (14 of them, without other psychiatric diagnoses, described in detail, from their therapists' observations and their own accounts of earlier attempts to stop; Gawin & Kleber, 1986), ending a binge is described as being followed by a crash: low mood mounting within 15 to 30 minutes of the last dose, with intense craving at first that faded if no more cocaine was available; then low mood, loss of pleasure, poor sleep, irritability, anxiety and confusion, ending 1 to 40 hours after use stopped, followed by 8 to 50 hours of heavy sleep with waking and overeating. The paper's figure gives the crash as 9 hours to 4 days, while the text says some people described up to 6 days. During the crash, 43% of the 14 had passing thoughts of suicide and 36% paranoia, both ending with the crash, and over 80% of those described had used sedatives, including alcohol or opioids, at least once to get to sleep. In the later part of the crash people described no craving: five people whose ordered cocaine arrived 2 to 5 hours after their last dose did not use it. A later controlled residential study found mood distress and craving at their highest on admission day, within 48 hours of last use, and falling from then on (Weddington et al., 1990). This is a description of what some people seeking treatment reported, which its authors call preliminary, limited by small numbers and by the lack of structured instruments or blind observation in parts of the study; with no comparison group, it cannot show how often a crash happens, how long it usually lasts, or what causes it. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: People who came for help with heavy cocaine use described a crash after a binge: very low mood and exhaustion, then a long, heavy sleep and a big appetite. It started soon after the last dose and usually ended within a few days. Some had thoughts of suicide or felt paranoid during the crash, and these passed when it ended; many had used alcohol or other drugs to get to sleep. This is what one clinic's patients reported, with no comparison group, so it cannot say how often it happens.
population: Adults seeking outpatient treatment for heavy binge cocaine use (DSM-III cocaine abuse) at one New Haven clinic in the early 1980s; 30 people, 14 described in detail
exposure: The end of a binge of cocaine use (intranasal, smoked or injected; study conditions in the study card)
comparator: None: a clinical description without a comparison group
outcome: Mood, craving, sleep and appetite in the hours and days after a binge (the crash), from clinicians' semistructured interviews and patients' accounts of earlier attempts to stop
magnitude: No rates beyond percentages of the 14 described in detail: passing suicidal thoughts 43%, paranoia 36%, both limited to the crash; over 80% had used alcohol or opioids to sleep. Durations: low mood from 15 to 30 minutes after the last dose, ending 1 to 40 hours after use stopped; heavy sleep 8 to 50 hours; crash 9 hours to 4 days in the figure, up to 6 days in the text.

evidence.locator: Subjects and Methods › Sample (p. 108); Procedures › Ratings and Raters (p. 109); Table 1 (p. 108)
evidence.extracted: Thirty consecutive self-referred outpatients (mean age 28.6, 73% men; 43% injected, 37% intranasal, 20% smoked) with heavy weekly use; raters were the treating therapists and were not blind to reports of cocaine use; abstinence was corroborated by urinalysis and by significant others.

evidence.locator: Clinical Findings › Abstinence Phenomenon, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Phase 1: Crash, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The course is described for the 14 people without other diagnoses, from observation and from accounts of earlier attempts to stop; when supplies ran out, low mood mounted within 15 to 30 minutes of the last dose with intense craving; the crash then brought low mood, loss of pleasure, insomnia, irritability, anxiety and confusion, ending one to 40 hours after use stopped, followed by eight to 50 hours of heavy sleep with waking and overeating; passing suicidal ideation (43% of the subsample) and paranoia (36%) were limited to this phase.

evidence.locator: Figure and legend (p. 110); Phase 1: Crash, 4th and 5th paragraphs (p. 111)
evidence.extracted: Craving was absent in the late crash and during heavy sleep; over 80% used sedatives (including alcohol or opiates) at least once to sleep; five people whose ordered cocaine arrived 2 to 5 hours after their last dose did not use it; eight people described a crash of at most 3 days and the rest up to 6 days, while the figure gives 9 hours to 4 days.

evidence.locator: Clinical Findings › Abstinence Symptoms and Diagnosis, 1st paragraph; Comment, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: All people with other diagnoses and four others were treated with medication, so the later phases were not observed without it in most; the authors call the findings preliminary, limited by small numbers and the lack of structured instruments or blind observation in parts of the study; editors' count: 20 of the 30 took medication.

evidence.locator: Results › Subject Characteristics, 3rd paragraph; Figure 1; Outcome › Mood Scores, Craving for Cocaine and Self-reports of Sleep (p. 864); Figure 2 and Table 2 (p. 865)
evidence.extracted: In a controlled residential study, all the men with cocaine dependence reported last using cocaine within 48 hours before admission; mood distress and craving were highest on admission day and fell over the 28 days (craving F = 17.270, P<.01); sleep reports did not differ from controls except more difficulty falling asleep and a greater improvement in clear-headedness on arising.

risk_of_bias.note: Therapists who were not blind, no standard rating of the crash, and timing partly from recollection of earlier attempts to stop.

inconsistency.note: Single description; the residential study's early measures do not conflict with it.

indirectness.note: Worded for people seeking treatment for heavy binge use at one clinic.

imprecision.note: Percentages of 14 people; no rates or ranges for most features.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim from a clinical case series starts low (METHODS §6.3). Measurement −1 (non-blind therapist raters, no standard rating, recollection) and imprecision −1 (percentages of 14 people) give very low. Status single study: only this series describes the crash; the residential study qualifies it (distress and craving were highest within 48 hours of last use) but did not measure the first hours after a binge.
